summary: Serbia keeps one of Europe's broadest visa-free regimes: EU, US, UK and most developed-country passports get 90 days in any 180, and — unusually — Russia, China, Belarus and the Gulf states enter visa-free too. Remaining nationalities apply for a visa at a Serbian embassy.

conditionalWaivers.text: Holders of a valid Schengen, US or UK visa — or a residence permit issued by one of those countries — can enter Serbia visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180-day period, regardless of nationality. The stay cannot exceed the validity of the visa you are traveling on.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Serbia

fee.notes: Approximate consular fee. Confirm the exact tariff with the Serbian embassy handling your application.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Serbia

fee.notes: Approximate fee for stays of 90–180 days for work, study or family reasons. Confirm with the Serbian embassy.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Serbia

passportValidity.text: Serbia requires a travel document valid at least 90 days beyond intended entry for visa applications; visa-free visitors should carry a passport valid comfortably beyond their stay. EU citizens and neighboring Balkan nationals can enter with a national ID card for short visits.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Serbia

travelInsurance.text: Not checked for visa-free entry, but visa applicants must show travel health insurance covering Serbia. EU EHIC cards are not valid in Serbia — private cover is recommended for all visitors.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Serbia

onwardTicket.text: Not systematically checked, but border police may ask about onward plans and accommodation.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Serbia

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is rigorously enforced; border police may ask visitors to show sufficient means — roughly €50 per day is the commonly cited benchmark.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Serbia

declarations.name: Address registration (white card)
declarations.text: All foreigners must be registered with the local police within 24 hours of arrival. Hotels do this automatically and issue a "white card"; if you stay privately, your host must register you at a police station. Keep the card. It can be checked on departure.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Serbia

currencyLimits.text: Cash of €10,000 or more (or equivalent) must be declared on entry and exit; undeclared amounts can be confiscated. Keep exchange receipts if you plan to re-convert larger sums of dinars when leaving.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Serbia

notes: Taking Serbian dinars out of the country is limited to RSD 120,000 per person — exchange leftover dinars before departure.

payments.text: Cards are accepted in practically all city shops, restaurants and supermarkets, but keep dinars for markets, kiosks, taxis and rural areas. Euros are not legal tender — exchange at banks or licensed exchange offices.

safety.text: Serbia is generally safe for visitors, and violent crime against tourists is rare. Watch for pickpocketing in central Belgrade, steer clear of football-fan gatherings, and avoid demonstrations, which occur periodically and can turn tense.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Serbia travel advice

bestTimeToVisit.text: May, June and September–October are pleasantly warm for Belgrade, Novi Sad and the monasteries; July is hot and lively around the EXIT and Guča festivals.

idp.text: Serbia is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either.

driving.text: Serbia is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Serbia yet.

tips.text: Do not enter Serbia directly from Kosovo unless you originally entered Kosovo from Serbia — without a Serbian entry stamp, Serbia treats arrival via Kosovo's other borders as illegal entry. Loop back the way you came.
Serbian border police may cancel or annotate Kosovo border stamps in your passport. It rarely causes travelers real problems, but avoid volunteering your Kosovo travel plans at the border.
You must be registered with the police within 24 hours of arrival — hotels handle it automatically, but private hosts must do it in person, and missing "white cards" can mean fines on exit.
Change money only at banks and licensed menjačnica exchange offices. Rates are good and commission-free. Never change money on the street.
Serbia is outside Schengen, so days spent here do not count against the 90/180 Schengen clock — one reason Belgrade is a popular long-stay and remote-work base.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Serbia?
faq.answer: Most visitors do not. Citizens of the EU, US, UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and most of Europe and the Americas enter visa-free for 90 days in any 180-day period, and Serbia also waives visas for Russia, China, Belarus and the Gulf states (30–90 days). Nationalities outside the waiver lists apply at a Serbian embassy.

faq.question: Can I enter Serbia from Kosovo?
faq.answer: Only if you first entered Kosovo from Serbia. Serbia does not treat Kosovo's borders with Albania, North Macedonia or Montenegro as international entry points into Serbia, so arriving that way leaves you without a Serbian entry stamp — treated as illegal entry. Enter Kosovo from Serbia and return the same way.

faq.question: How long can Russian citizens stay in Serbia?
faq.answer: Russian passport holders enter visa-free for up to 30 days per visit under the bilateral agreement. Many long-stayers reset the clock with a border run to a neighboring country, but for genuine long stays a temporary residence permit is the proper route.

faq.question: Can EU citizens enter Serbia with just an ID card?
faq.answer: Yes — EU citizens can enter Serbia for short stays with a valid national ID card instead of a passport, as can citizens of several neighboring Balkan states. Carrying a passport is still recommended for hotel registration and onward travel.

faq.question: Is Serbia in the EU or Schengen?
faq.answer: No — Serbia is an EU candidate but belongs to neither the EU nor Schengen. Time spent in Serbia does not count against your 90/180-day Schengen allowance, and you will get full entry and exit stamps at the border.

faq.question: Do I have to register with the police in Serbia?
faq.answer: Yes, within 24 hours of arrival. Hotels and hostels register you automatically and give you a small "white card"; if you stay in a private apartment, your host must register you at the local police station. Keep the card until you leave.
